slides.page_title: Query Planning & The Router At Runtime

blocks.title: No Restart
blocks.text: With Uplink or `--hot-reload`, the router swaps in a new supergraph in place. Schema change never means a gateway redeploy — that alone justifies the pipeline.

items: Router parses the operation, plans against the supergraph, runs it
Planning is a search over possible subgraph paths
Scored by number of fetches and depth of the chain
CPU-heavy when cold, which is why plans are cached
The plan cache keys on the ==normalized operation==
Cold plans on a large schema cost tens of ms
Persisted queries shrink the request; the plan cache skips planning
Step 1 always hits a subgraph owning a root field
Headers propagate only if configured; every subgraph re-authorizes
Timeouts and circuit breaking live in the router
Cost and depth limits run **before** planning
One client query becomes N OpenTelemetry spans

blocks.title: Partial Failure
blocks.text: One subgraph 500s and you get valid `data` with null holes plus an `errors` entry. No retries by default, and a non-null field nulls its nearest nullable ancestor.

caption.text: Part 3 of GRAPHQL FEDERATION. One endpoint for clients, ten teams shipping independently — that is the whole pitch of GraphQL federation, and the bill arrives in round trips. This handbook walks the full path: subgraph anatomy, `@key` design, reference resolvers and the N+1 they hide, every field directive, composition errors decoded, how the router actually plans a query, and an honest comparison against schema stitching. Ends with a three-subgraph supergraph you can read line by line.
